etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English witnesse, from Old English ġewitnes, equivalent to wit +‎ -ness. Cognate with Middle Dutch wetenisse (“witness, testimony”), Old High German gewiznessi (“testimony”), Icelandic vitni (“witness”).

definitions.definition: (uncountable) Attestation of a fact or event; testimony.

quote.citation: c. 1597 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Merry Wiues of Windsor”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene ii]:
quote.text: May we, with the warrant of womanhood and the witness of a good conscience, pursue him with any further revenge?

quote.citation: 1959, Alexander MacLaren, Expositions of holy scripture‎[1], volume 6:
quote.text: We have as much witness from heaven as we need.

quote.citation: 1999, Nettie Becker, Paul Becker, A Comprehensive Guide for Caregivers in Day-care Settings‎[2]:
quote.text: On another corner, stands an old style tenement building, whose dirty grey facade bears as much witness to the volume of exhaust fumes from millions of passing cars as it does to the age of the dwelling.

quote.citation: 2002, Charles E. Scott, The Lives of Things‎[3], page 125:
quote.text: Nor do the formation and articulation of such knowledge themselves bear much witness to Geist.

quote.citation: 2008, Jeremiah Burroughs, C. Matthew McMahon, Therese B. McMahon, The Excellency of Holy Courage in Evil Times‎[4], page 100:
quote.text: Fleeing is giving witness, and those that plead against it are loath to give so much witness

quote.citation: 2014, James Tarter, God's Word to the United States: The Book of Obadiah‎[5]:
quote.text: Ob. 16 can show that every nation will get at least this much witness

definitions.definition: (countable) One who sees or has personal knowledge of something.

quote.citation: c. 1590–1591 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Two Gentlemen of Verona”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene ii]:
quote.text: […] thyself art witness— I am betrothed.
Upon my looking round, I was a witness to appearances which filled me with melancholy and regret.

definitions.definition: (countable, law) Someone called to give evidence in a court.

quote.citation: 1961 November, “Talking of Trains: Derailment near Holmes Chapel”, in Trains Illustrated, page 652:
quote.text: From the evidence of witnesses and of the recorded passing times, including the time at which the circuit breakers were tripped when the wires were brought down, the train was travelling at a speed of not less than 70 m.p.h.

definitions.definition: (countable) One who is called upon to witness an event or action, such as a wedding or the signing of a document.
(countable) Something that serves as evidence; a sign or token.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Genesis 31:51-52:
quote.text: Laban said to Jacob,  […]  This heap be witness, and this pillar be witness.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To furnish proof of, to show.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book I”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC, lines 56-57:
quote.text: round he throws his baleful eyes / That witness'd huge affliction and dismay

quote.citation: 1993, Vicki M. Pino, “Viewpoints from our Readers after "Aprongate": Lighten up”, in Atlanta Journal Constitution:
quote.text: Depression often goes undetected until it is too late . Witness the recent White House suicide.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To see or gain knowledge of through experience.

quote.text: This is but a faint sketch of the incalculable calamities and horrors we must expect, should we be so unfortunate as ever to witness the triumph of modern infidelity

quote.citation: 1803, John Marshall, The Life of George Washington:
quote.text: General Washington did not live to witness the restoration of peace.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, construed with to or for) To present personal religious testimony; to preach at (someone) or on behalf of.

quote.citation: 1998, Routledge Encyclopedia of Philosophy, volume 6, "Niebuhr, Reinhold", page 842:
quote.text: Instead, Niebuhr's God was the God witnessed to in the Hebrew Scriptures and the New Testament, the Bible of the Christian world.

definitions.definition: To see the execution of (a legal instrument), and subscribe it for the purpose of establishing its authenticity.
